title: The media: internet and email
subtitle: browse, upload, attachment, spam
summary: Discuss the pros and cons of the internet with precise vocabulary - from webinars, file-sharing and e-commerce to spam, cookies and parental controls.

lesson.heading: The pros: talking to people
lesson.text: Email is only the beginning. **Instant messaging** is a kind of email where both people are online at the same time. A **chat room** is an online conversation between a group of people on topics they choose, which you can enter or leave at any time. A **newsgroup** is a website where people with shared interests get news and information, and **social networking sites** let you connect with other people, make new friends and keep up with their personal news.

examples.text: We settled the whole thing in five minutes of **instant messaging**.
If you **subscribe to** newsgroups, you often get hundreds of messages.
examples.note: subscribe to = become a member of

examples.text: She often **posts** ridiculous details about her life on **social networking sites**.
examples.note: post = add material to a site

lesson.heading: The pros: doing things online
lesson.text: **E-commerce** covers all kinds of business done on the internet, such as internet banking and travel booking, and there are **e-books**, **e-learning** and **webinars** - online seminars. You can **browse**, which is looking at different websites with no particular goal, or **surf the web**, moving from page to page usually looking for something.

examples.text: Half the fun is just **browsing** and **surfing the web**.
We have **e-enabled** everything you need to study online.
examples.note: e-enabled = made available to work with over the internet

examples.text: **E-signatures** now have the same legal status as handwritten ones.
The **dotcom** economy has attracted hundreds of new businesses hoping to make a fortune.

lesson.heading: Sending and sharing
lesson.text: You can **transfer graphic images** - the technical term for pictures, icons and diagrams - and sound files. Files sent with an email message are **attachments**, and **file-sharing** is the practice of sharing computer data or space on a network. You **download** files to your computer and **upload** them from it.

examples.text: I'll send you the figures as an **attachment**.
**Download** and **upload** times can be painfully slow.
**Gaming** means you can play video games with anyone in the world.

lesson.heading: The cons
lesson.text: **ISP** charges - Internet Service Provider, pronounced letter by letter - can be high for heavy users. People you have never met may get your contact details, and your account may be **hacked**, that is accessed illegally. **Spam**, also called **junk mail**, is unwanted advertising sent to you by email, and **cookies** are pieces of software that follow and record what you do and which sites you visit.

examples.text: My account was **hacked** and everyone in my address book got **spam** from me.
Some ISPs allow you to **screen out** or **filter out** unwanted mail.
examples.note: screen out / filter out = prevent from reaching you

examples.text: The internet can become **addictive** - something you cannot stop doing.

lesson.heading: Offensive material and parental control
lesson.text: Many sites contain **offensive material**: pornography, extreme political views, or material that encourages hate and violence against people. **Parental control** is the ability of parents to decide which websites their children can visit and to restrict certain activities.

examples.text: **Parental controls** provided by ISPs are vital these days.
E-learners may miss a 'live' teacher, and **e-books** don't feel the same as real books.

lesson.heading: Opposites in computer English
rows: yes - restore something you erased by accident
no - there is no such word

lesson.heading: Things that go wrong
lesson.text: Your **server** - the central computer that distributes email and other services to a group of users - can be **down**, which means not working. An email to a dead address **bounces**, or comes back to you. And good **anti-virus software**, protection against computer viruses, is worth updating frequently.

examples.text: Our **server** at work was **down** yesterday, so I didn't get your message till today.
She must have changed her email address - the email I sent her **bounced**.
I've **bookmarked** the CNN home page, as I use it regularly.
examples.note: bookmark = put in a list of sites you can reach immediately

lesson.text: Browsing has no goal and surfing usually has one - you browse for pleasure, you surf looking for something.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with its explanation.

pairs.right: a site where people with common interests talk online
a sort of class held live on the web
a company that gives you access to the internet
a program that follows your activities on the web
a file sent at the same time as an email message
unwanted advertising sent to you by email

exercises.prompt: I've had your message in my ___ for two days, but haven't had time to read it yet.
exercises.explanation: Mail arrives in your inbox; mail waiting to be sent sits in your outbox.

exercises.prompt: I sent a photo of my house to a friend in Canada, but it took ages to ___ .
exercises.explanation: You upload files from your computer to the internet and download files to it.

exercises.prompt: I spent nearly five minutes ___ just waiting for that photo to go.
exercises.explanation: Online means connected to the internet; offline means disconnected.

exercises.prompt: I had a lot of trouble trying to ___ that new software I bought.
exercises.hint: (add to the programs on your computer)
exercises.explanation: You install software and uninstall it when you no longer want it.

exercises.prompt: How do I ___ a file on this computer?
exercises.explanation: Undelete is the opposite of delete: it brings back something you erased by mistake.

exercises.prompt: I edit my pictures ___ and then connect to send them.
exercises.explanation: Offline is the opposite of online.

exercises.prompt: This is an old version of the software. You can ___ it online for free.
exercises.explanation: You update software to a newer version - there is no verb downdate.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is NOT a real word in computer English?
exercises.explanation: Update has no opposite downdate; the other three all exist.

exercises.prompt: 'E-learning will become more and more common.' What is e-learning?
options: taking courses over the internet instead of at a school or college
learning how to use a computer
learning a language by email only
an electronic test at the end of a course
exercises.explanation: The prefix e- means done over the internet: e-learning, e-commerce, e-books.

exercises.prompt: 'With this smartphone you'll never need a tablet or a laptop.' What is a tablet here?
options: a very thin portable computer used mostly for email and online activities
a small notebook for writing things down
a paid app for reading books
a keyboard you attach to a phone
exercises.explanation: A tablet is a thin, often quite small portable computer, used mainly for email and online activities.

exercises.statement: If an email bounces, it means the person has read it and replied immediately.
exercises.explanation: An email that bounces comes back to you undelivered, often because the address has changed.

exercises.statement: If your server is down, you cannot receive your email.
exercises.explanation: The server is the central computer that distributes email; down means not working.

exercises.prompt: Is each thing usually presented as a pro or a con of internet use?
